meta.title: Data protection for a small clinic
meta.description: A plain guide to UK GDPR for a five-person physiotherapy practice: what data we hold, why we may hold it, answering access requests and handling a breach.
meta.author: Brightwater Physiotherapy, practice manager

summary: We hold contact, payment and health records for about 2,300 patients; health data is special category data and needs extra care. Each kind of data has a lawful basis written down before we collect it. A patient who asks for their data gets it free within one month, and a breach that risks patients' rights is reported to the ICO within 72 hours of us becoming aware of it.

meta.question: What personal data do we hold, and where?
meta.title: What we hold

answer.headline: We hold personal data on about 2,300 patients and 5 staff across four systems; the clinical notes are health data, which UK GDPR treats as special category and protects most strictly.
answer.text: You cannot protect data you do not know you have. This map is our record of processing: the ICO expects one, and it is the starting point for every other chapter.
points: Clinical notes, booking details and invoices are the main records
Paper intake forms are scanned and shredded within 7 days
Records are kept 8 years after a patient's last appointment, then deleted

blocks.title: Our record of processing
rows: Name, phone, email, date of birth

blocks.title: Records by system
blocks.caption: Count of people with a record in each system, October 2026.

items.title: Special category
items.text: Health data needs a lawful basis *and* a separate condition under Article 9, such as providing health care.

items.title: Higher harm
items.text: A leak of clinical notes can cause real distress, so breaches are more likely to be reportable.

items.title: Confidentiality duty
items.text: As health professionals we also owe patients a duty of confidence, separate from GDPR.

blocks.title: We pay the ICO fee
blocks.label: Housekeeping
blocks.body: Most organisations that process personal data must pay the ICO an annual data protection fee. Ours renews every March; the practice manager holds the reminder.

meta.question: What gives us the right to use each kind of data?
meta.title: Lawful basis

answer.headline: Each use of personal data needs one of six lawful bases, chosen before we start. For us, treatment rests on contract, invoices on legal obligation and the newsletter on consent.
answer.text: The basis is not a box-ticking label: it decides what rights the patient has and what we must do if they object. Consent is often the wrong choice, because a patient can withdraw it at any time.
points: Treating patients: contract, plus the health care condition for health data
Keeping invoices: legal obligation (HMRC requires 6 years)
Newsletter: consent, with a clear opt-in and an easy way out

blocks.title: The six lawful bases
rows: The person has a real choice and can say no without losing out
You need the data to provide what they asked for
A law requires you to process it
You carry out a public function
Not used: we are a private clinic
A balanced, expected use that does not override their rights

options.name: Consent
options.summary: Ask every patient to tick a box.
cons: Reminders stop if consent is withdrawn
We must record and refresh every consent

options.name: Legitimate interests
options.summary: Reminders are expected and help the patient.
cons: Needs a short written balancing test
Patients can still object, and we must stop

blocks.title: Do not switch basis later
blocks.label: Common mistake
blocks.body: If you rely on consent and it is withdrawn, you cannot quietly switch to legitimate interests to carry on. Pick the right basis at the start and tell people in the privacy notice.

items.text: Write down what the data is for and the lawful basis
For health data, note the Article 9 condition as well
Update the privacy notice on the website and intake form
Add the new data to the record of processing

meta.question: What do we do when a patient asks for a copy of their data?
meta.title: Subject access requests

answer.headline: Confirm who they are, find everything we hold about them and send a copy free of charge within one calendar month of receiving the request.
answer.text: A request does not need a form or the words 'subject access': an email, a letter or a remark at reception all count. The clock starts the day we receive it, not the day the right person notices.
points: One month, extendable by two more only for complex or numerous requests
Usually free; a reasonable fee only if a request is manifestly unfounded or excessive
Remove other people's personal data before sending, unless they agree

items.title: Log it the same day
items.text: Add it to the request log with the date received. The deadline is the same date next month.

items.title: Check identity
items.text: Ask for ID only if we are unsure who they are. The clock pauses until we have it.

items.title: Search every system
items.text: Booking, clinical notes, accounts, email and the paper archive.

items.title: Redact
items.text: Remove details about other people, such as a family member mentioned in notes.

items.title: Send securely
items.text: Encrypted email or a printed copy collected in person, with a cover letter explaining what is included.

items.q: A parent asks for their 15-year-old's records. Do we send them?
items.a: Not automatically. A child who understands their rights can make their own request, and we should consider their wishes. Ask the child, and take advice if unsure.

items.q: A solicitor asks for a patient's notes for a claim.
items.a: Ask for the patient's signed authority. With it, treat it as the patient's own request.

items.q: Could releasing a note cause serious harm to the patient?
items.a: Health data has a narrow exemption where disclosure would be likely to cause serious harm. The treating physiotherapist must decide, and we record why.

meta.question: What do we do if personal data is lost, stolen or sent to the wrong person?
meta.title: Breaches

answer.headline: Contain it, assess the risk to patients and, if it is likely to harm their rights, report it to the ICO within 72 hours of becoming aware. Tell the patients directly if the risk is high.
answer.text: A breach is any loss of confidentiality, integrity or availability of personal data: an email to the wrong address, a stolen laptop or ransomware locking the notes. Every breach goes in our breach log, even ones we do not report.
points: The 72 hours include weekends and bank holidays
We can report what we know and add detail later
Not reporting a reportable breach can lead to a fine

items.title: Someone notices
items.text: Tell the practice manager at once, by phone if out of hours.

items.title: Contain
items.text: Recall the email, ask the recipient to delete it, change passwords or isolate the device.

items.title: Assess
items.text: Whose data, how sensitive, how many people, and what could happen to them.

items.title: Decide
items.text: Reportable or not, recorded with the reasons in the breach log.

items.title: Report
items.text: Report to the ICO online or by phone, and contact affected patients if the risk is high.

blocks.title: Report it or not?
rows: Appointment time emailed to the wrong patient, deleted on request
Unencrypted laptop with clinical notes stolen
Encrypted laptop stolen, key not with it
Ransomware locks notes for two days, backups restore them

blocks.title: Encryption is the cheapest protection
blocks.label: Prevention
blocks.body: All laptops and phones that hold patient data use full-disk encryption and a screen lock. A lost encrypted device is a log entry; a lost unencrypted one is a report to the ICO and a letter to every patient on it.
